# Trichy assault rifle
## Development and Design
The Trichy assault rifle (TAR) is a 7.62 × 39 mm assault rifle developed by the Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) in India. Initiated in the early 2010s, the project aimed to create an indigenous counterpart to the AK-47, reducing reliance on imported rifles. An early version of the rifle was unveiled in 2011, when OFT officials announced a locally designed 7.62 mm weapon “matching the specifications of the AK-47”. It was subsequently named the Trichy Assault Rifle to honor the factory’s contribution. After successful field trials (including evaluation by the Indian Army) and iterative improvements, the rifle entered production by late 2016. The first batch was delivered in March 2017 to the Chhattisgarh state police for use in anti-insurgency operations.
The Trichy assault rifle is a selective-fire weapon chambered for the 7.62 × 39 mm cartridge – the same ammunition used in Kalashnikov rifles. It operates in semi-automatic and automatic (burst-fire) modes, with a cyclic rate of fire of approximately 600 rounds per minute. The rifle’s effective range is around 300 meters, with a maximum effective distance of up to 500 meters for area targets. Notably, unlike many AK-47 variants that use stamped sheet-metal receivers, the TAR is built with a fully machined (milled) steel receiver for improved strength and durability. It supports a 30-round curved magazine and can mount accessories such as optical sights and under-barrel grenade launchers. OFT’s design explicitly allows integration of 40 mm UBGL units (including the 40×46 mm M6 launcher), enhancing the rifle’s versatility for firing grenades or tear-gas shells. The rifle also features a foldable buttstock (in certain variants) and Picatinny rails on the fore-end for mounting scopes or night sights, according to user requirements.
## Variants
OFT produces the Trichy assault rifle in several configurations to meet different user needs. Initially, three main stock variants were offered: a model with a fixed (non-folding) butt, one with a side-folding buttstock, and one with an under-folding stock. All versions share the same internal mechanism and caliber, and all can be equipped with the 40 mm under-barrel grenade launcher attachment. In August 2021, OFT formally launched the under-folding stock variant (described as a “down-folding butt” model) to provide a more compact profile for troops on patrolling and guard duties. By this time a fourth version with a telescoping (retractable) buttstock had also been developed, bringing the total to four stock options. These folding and telescoping-stock models allow the weapon to be shortened for transport or close-quarters use, improving handling in tight spaces (e.g. inside vehicles or buildings). Apart from stock configuration, the core specifications remain consistent across variants.
### TriCa compact carbine
In 2021, OFT introduced a shortened carbine derivative of the rifle, nicknamed the “Baby TAR” or TriCa (Trichy Carbine). The TriCa is a compact assault carbine designed for close-quarters situations and for personnel who need a smaller weapon. It has a significantly reduced barrel length (about 210 mm or 8.3 inches, roughly half the standard AK-47 barrel) which cuts the effective range to roughly 150–175 m. The TriCa retains the same 7.62×39 mm chambering and uses standard AK-type 30-round magazines, ensuring ammunition commonality with the full-size TAR. To compensate for the shorter barrel, the weapon includes an improved flash suppressor and internal design tweaks to reduce muzzle flash and overheating when firing rapidly from the short barrel. The TriCa is lightweight and highly portable – only 19 inches (49 cm) long with the stock folded, and weighing about 3.5 kg with a loaded magazine. This makes it roughly 1 kg lighter than a full-size AK-47. According to OFT, the compact carbine is well-suited for special forces, vehicle and aircraft crews, police commando units, and security personnel guarding high-value installations.
After internal development during 2020, the TriCa underwent trials (including informal evaluations by Army units) where prototypes reportedly fired thousands of rounds without malfunctions. It was officially released in mid-2021 and began attracting orders from law enforcement. For example, the Kerala Police ordered 92 TriCa carbines in 2022 and received their first consignment in May 2025. Other agencies such as the Assam Forest Department and the Central Bureau of Narcotics have also placed orders for the weapon as of 2025. The introduction of the TriCa adds a domestically-produced option for a compact 7.62 mm weapon, filling a niche for high-firepower yet concealable arms in India’s security forces.
## Service and Adoption
Although developed with military standards in mind, the Trichy assault rifle has been primarily adopted by India’s central armed police and state police forces rather than the regular Army. The first users were police units engaged in counterinsurgency: the Chhattisgarh state police received an initial batch of 200 rifles in early 2017 for anti-Naxalite operations. Following its debut, multiple states – including Jharkhand, Rajasthan, and Madhya Pradesh – placed orders as they modernized their armouries, and the rifle was observed in field use during security operations by those forces.
At the national level, the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) – India’s largest paramilitary police force – conducted extensive trials of the TAR around 2017–2018. These tests involved evaluating accuracy, reliability, and environmental robustness (drop tests, mud and water immersion, extreme weather firing, etc.). The TAR reportedly passed a 15,000-round endurance test “without any single stoppage,” demonstrating its reliability in sustained fire. Satisfied with performance, the CRPF first ordered a pilot batch of 100 rifles, and after positive field feedback (including use in varied terrains such as Jammu & Kashmir), the CRPF placed a bulk order for 6,167 rifles in 2018–2019. The first installment of this order (500 rifles) was handed over to CRPF in March 2020.
Other central forces soon followed. The Border Security Force (BSF) and the Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) together requisitioned about 17,000 Trichy rifles by 2020 to re-equip their units guarding India’s frontiers. By that time, OFT reported that approximately 11,000 TAR units had already been delivered across various police and paramilitary organizations nationwide. According to media reports in 2021, the cumulative production of Trichy rifles neared 20,000 units supplied to Indian security forces. Notably, the rifle is being used to replace obsolete .303 Lee–Enfield bolt-action rifles and older 7.62 mm self-loading rifles in many police inventories. For instance, in 2025 Kolkata Police announced the induction of new Trichy Assault Rifles to finally phase out their WWII-era .303 rifles as part of a modernization drive. Senior officers there cited the TAR’s lighter weight (~3.5 kg, about 2 kg less than a .303) and its 500 m effective range with burst-fire as major advantages for urban policing.
The Indian Army, while having tested the Trichy assault rifle, did not formally procure it for standard infantry use – instead pursuing other rifle procurement programs (such as the import of SIG Sauer 7.62 mm rifles and co-production of AK-203 rifles with Russia). Thus, the TAR’s impact has been most visible among internal security forces. Its adoption by the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) and state police units contributes to India’s Atmanirbhar (self-reliance) initiative in small arms, by providing a locally-made alternative to the many AK-style rifles that were previously imported for police and paramilitary needs. In fact, the Trichy rifle’s design is heavily based on the Bulgarian Arsenal AR-M1 (a licensed AK-47 variant), thousands of which were procured by Indian agencies in the past. The TAR now offers an indigenous substitute: each unit costs the government significantly less than an imported rifle (approximately ₹55,000 for a TAR vs. ₹75,000 for a new AK-203 in 2021). The introduction of the Trichy assault rifle and its carbine variant has therefore been a strategic step toward modernizing India’s police arsenals with Made-in-India firearms while reducing dependency on foreign suppliers.

TIRUCHY : Addressing the need for high calibre, light weight weapons for paramilitary forces battling insurgents, Ordnance Factory Tiruchirapalli (OFT) has developed an assault rifle that is on par the iconic AK 47 rifle. The first batch of rifles was handed over to Chattisgarh police on Saturday.

Said to match the AK-47, the indigenously designed and developed 7.62X39 mm rifle is touted as substitute to the former and save valuable foreign exchange by reducing dependence on imports.

The rifle can be operated both in automatic and single fire modes and has been developed specifically to address operational requirements of forces deployed in naxalite-prone States.

“The weapon can fire up to 600 rounds a minute in automatic mode. Targets at a distance of 500m can be destroyed and the assault rifle is highly effective up to a distance of 300m.

We have orders to produce 4,000 units for four State police departments including Chattisgarh,” said K Appa Rao, general manager, OFT. The weapon is an outcome of 1.5 years of R&D and is available in three variants – fixed butt, side foldable, and under folding versions. All three models can be mounted with a 40mm under barrel grenade launcher.

Stating that OFT has been modernising the plant to match the evolving requirements of Armed forces, Rao said additional assembly lines were being established to ramp up production.

Kolkata Police are set to phase out their decades-old .303 guns and replace them with modern assault rifles developed by the Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli. The new Trichy Assault Rifles (TAR), modelled on the Bulgarian AR-M1 and described as an indigenous variant of the AK-47, are expected to arrive in batches early next year. “The consignment will reach in phases, and distribution will begin soon after,” an officer of the rank of deputy commissioner of Kolkata Police said. ADVERTISEMENT One of the biggest advantages is weight, senior officers said. The old .303 rifles weigh about 5.5kg, while the TAR is at least 2kg lighter. The officers said the rifle supports both single-shot and burst fire, allowing accurate engagement of targets up to 500 metres. “Its lightweight modular design and foldable butt make it handy, even for guard and patrolling duty,” a senior officer said. Chhattisgarh Police deployed the weapon during anti-Naxalite operations earlier this year, while Rajasthan, Jharkhand, and Madhya Pradesh police forces have also procured it, sources said. Officers across units said such upgrades bolster not just capability but morale. “If one has to face a barrage of bullets from terrorists or armed criminals, modern firearms are essential. 'Baby TAR', India’s smallest assault rifle

[![Image 4: Sandeep Unnithan](https://akm-img-a-in.tosshub.com/indiatoday/images/reporter/201901/image005_0-770x433-profile_image_one_to_one_1.jpg?VersionId=.pasKkvdD84ULmLha3vENVAV69BnJMOd&size=50:50)](https://www.indiatoday.in/author/sandeep-unnithan "Sandeep Unnithan")

![Image 5](https://akm-img-a-in.tosshub.com/indiatoday/images/mediamanager/india_today_insight.jpg?IzvocAu7gyMv.UA3nBmTl5xRnm990vx3)It’s laptop-sized, can be carried inside a coat and can spit AK-47 bullets out at the rate of roughly 700 rounds per minute. Meet the ‘Baby TAR’, India’s smallest assault rifle. Developed by the Indian Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappali, the weapon is a compact version of the legendary AK-47, which the factory has been mass-producing since 2017. This in-house OFB innovation comes soon after the Indian Army unveiled a 9x19mm carbine developed in-house.

advertisement

The TAR-3, a compact, fully automatic version of the Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), recently passed a series of trials at the Ordnance Factory Trichy (OF Trichy). A dozen prototypes have been produced during the lockdown. The weapon is currently undergoing ‘unofficial trials’ with the Indian Army, where three prototypes are believed to have fired over 2,000 rounds each without stoppages.

The ‘Baby TAR’ fires the same 7.62x39 mm cartridge as the AK-47—this ammunition is in widespread production and use, thereby easing logistics. It uses the AK-47’s distinctive 30-round curved box magazine and features a commonality of parts with existing weapons. Its designers chopped down the AK-47’s 16-inch barrel, producing a weapon with an 8.3-inch barrel and an effective range of 150 metres. The TAR-3 is 19.2 inches long with its stock folded, and at 2.7 kg (unloaded), is one kg lighter than the AK-47. It has a monoblock receiver, shockproof polymer lower parts and two Picatinny rails that can mount a variety of sights and scopes.

ALSO READ | [The Indian Army’s ‘General Kalashnikov’ gives it a new 9 mm sub-machine gun](https://www.indiatoday.in/india-today-insight/story/the-indian-army-s-general-kalashnikov-gives-it-a-new-9-mm-sub-machine-gun-1759202-2021-01-14)

Its designers say it is ideal for users like special forces and counter-terrorist operators who want compact, concealable weapons but with the firepower of a full-sized AK-47. The assault rifle is also suitable for aircraft, tank and vehicle crews. Significantly, the weapon was developed as an unsolicited design—without waiting for army General Staff Qualitative Requirements (GSQRs), which usually is the start point for weapon development. To do so, the factory used the experience it gained from mass producing the Trichy Assault Rifle, a wholly indigenous copy of the AK-47.

Designers at OF Trichy appear to have solved a problem that stumped the gun designers of the DRDO’s now-discarded INSAS carbine variant in the 1990s—how to reduce the barrel heating and the excessive sound and flash produced when an assault rifle bullet is fired from a short barrel. The DRDO did it by switching over to a smaller bullet, the 5.56x30 round used in the JVPC carbine. The Baby TAR designers solved the problem by used internal metal reflectors to insulate the foregrip from the barrel and by designing, in-house, a compact flash hider at the barrel muzzle. The gun can presently fire four full magazines—around 120 rounds—without the barrel heating. This development is noteworthy because it means Indian designers now understand the ‘know-why’, rather than just the ‘know-how’ that they would have gained from a licensed production.

advertisement

**Compacting the AK**

The Soviet Union began producing compact, stubbier versions of its AK-74 rifle (an AK-47 evolution firing the 5.45x39 mm cartridge) in the 1970s. Copies of this compact assault rifle have been famously attached to Osama bin Laden, ISIS chief Abu Bakr Al Baghdadi and more recently, Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko. Compact versions of the AK-47 believed to have been produced in the frontier regions of Pakistan, have been recovered by Indian security forces from terrorists in Jammu and Kashmir in recent months.

Trichy is one of two Indian ordnance factories already mass-producing Indian versions of the legendary Kalashnikov (the original weapon was never patented and is freely made by countries across the world). The ‘Ghatak’, a copy made by Rifle Factory Ishapore, did not find as much favour. The full-sized TAR is believed to be a copy of the Bulgarian AR-M1, itself a licensed copy of the Kalashnikov. Over 500,000 Bulgarian weapons have been imported by India’s central, state and paramilitary forces over the past decade—the TAR, which began bulk production in 2017, has also helped reducing imports from that east European country. OF Trichy has developed four variants of the rifle, with fixed, side-folding, under-folding and telescoping butts. Nearly 20,000 weapons have been delivered to the Indian police, paramilitary and central armed police forces. Interestingly, each TAR costs around Rs 55,000—far less than the licensed AK-203 to be produced by Indo-Russian Rifles, which will cost upwards of Rs 75,000. And the compact version could cost less than the full-length TAR.

advertisement

The compact TAR’s arrival has added to growing numbers of indigenously designed small arms. From a virtual drought a few years back, there are now multiple indigenous designs available, chambered for various cartridges. Besides the Army’s 9x19mm carbine, the DRDO has developed a variant firing a 5.56x45 mm cartridge, for a different Army requirement. The JVPC, a DRDO-OFB carbine, passed Army and MHA development trials last year. Bengaluru-based small arms start up SSS Defence has its own designs for weapons, chambered for 5.56x45 and 7.62x39 cartridges, and an upgrade kit for existing AK-47 variants. All these designs, of course, are at the prototype stage and will need to fire several thousand rounds before they are fit for mass-production and induction.

Tiruchi Assault Rifle (image: Youtube)

Tiruchi Assault Rifle (TAR), developed by the India's Ordnance Factory Tiruchirapalli (OFT) has been handed over to the Border Security Force for the first time on Sunday.

The 7.62×39 mm rifle had undergone a series of tests and had been supplied earlier to police departments of states. It has been approved for use by the paramilitary force for the first time.

The rifle is touted to be an improved version of INSAS rifle and it is similar to the AK-47 series. The weapon is suitable for paramilitary forces deployed for quelling insurgency.

The weapon has a maximum range of 500 metres. In automatic mode, it fires 600 rounds per minute. The design is compatible for attachment with a 40mm under barrel Grenade Launcher UBGL and 40x46 mm under barrel Grenade Launcher UBGL-M6, according to OFT.

The rifle manufactured in three variants: fixed butt, side foldable butt and under folding uses ammunition made by Ordnance Factory, Varangoan, Bhushawal.

![Image 2: OFT hands over first batch of 500 Trichy Assault Rifles to CRPF](https://static.toiimg.com/thumb/msid-47529300,imgsize-110164,width-400,height-225,resizemode-72/47529300.jpg)

Trichy: The first batch of 500 Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) indigenously developed by the Ordnance Factory of Tiruchirappalli (OFT) was handed over to the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) at the factory premises on Thursday. The rifles are part of the total order for 6,167 rifles. OFT here has so far supplied around 11,000 TARs to various central and state police forces.

![Image 3: 1x1 polls](https://static.toiimg.com/photo/25581306.cms)

The rifles were received by CRPF DIG D S Rawat.  
Trichy Assault Rifle was conceived in 2015 and production began at OFT in 2017. TAR, is considered an equivalent variant of AK-47. Compared to stamped sheet metal riveted body in other rifles, TAR features a fully machined receiver body for higher reliability and strength.  
After Chhattisgarh state police received the first batch of 200 TARs in March 2017, various state police forces and paramilitary forces placed orders for the rifle. CRPF had conducted evaluation trials of TAR including accuracy and reliability apart from tests such as drop, mud, saltwater immersion and rain tests. The rifle was then subjected to life cycle test in which 15,000 rounds were fired without any single stoppage, proving its reliability. After successful trials, CRPF placed a pilot order for 100 rifles.  
After extensive field usage in various terrains including Srinagar, in 2018, CRPF placed the bulk order. CRPF had asked for customised requirements such as upper hand guard with picatinny rail for mounting telescopes and tritium filled luminous sources for night firing capability.  

“Our factory has produced several weapons. Among all, TAR is undoubtedly our biggest success,” said Shirish Khare, general manager, OFT.  
The ordnance factory here has 17,000 orders for TAR from Border Security Force and Sashastra Seema Bal.

Trichy: Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) handed over 92 TriCa (Trichy Carbine 7.62x39 mm), a mini version of Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), to the Kerala police force on Friday. This is the first delivery of the rifles from OFT, a unit of Advanced Weapons & Equipment India Limited (AWEIL) functioning under the ministry of defence. Executive director Sanjay Shrivastava along with general managers flagged off the vehicle carrying the weapons to Kerala. TriCa is an indigenously developed weapon. OFT said that TriCa has the size of a typical submachine gun, weighing 3.5kg (with magazine) and with a firing range of up to 175m. It is a light and compact weapon designed for the crews of infantry combat vehicles, helicopters, paratroopers, police personnel, personnel guarding high secure buildings including airports, and special operation forces.TriCa was first released by the factory in July 2021, and the Kerala police placed the order for 92 rifles in 2022. As of May 2025, OFT said it has received orders from Assam forest and Central Bureau of Narcotics (CBN) units for the weapon. Besides, TAR and TriCa, OFT has also been manufacturing the 12.7mm stabilised remote control gun (SRCG) system.
